A woman posted that her period came back after just 11 days on carnivore, and the replies turned into this incredible thread of women sharing hormone recovery stories. If you missed Sarah's piece on getting your electrolytes right, it's a perfect companion to what Dr. Tony Hampton dropped on YouTube this week about LMNT and Re-Lyte. On the YouTube side, Keto Twins are everywhere right now. Their keto dessert video pulled 20K views and the comments turned into a recipe workshop, with people swapping cookie brands and sharing allulose hacks for ice cream that doesn't freeze rock-solid. Their eating out guide hit 16K views and honestly the comment section reads like a crowdsourced restaurant survival manual. People are ordering crustless pizza bowls, taco salads without the shell, and sushi rolls without rice. Meanwhile Kent Carnivore tackled the "low protein is healthiest" claim that's been floating around longevity circles, and Ground Beef Chief introduced his girlfriend at Week 74 of his journey. The comment "your heart rate was high cos you're in love" got 20 likes. That's the kind of content that makes you remember why this community is different. The funniest post of the week? Someone complaining that the most annoying part of carnivore is that none of their clothes fit anymore. 236 upvotes. One person said they went from 2XL to XL, bought a whole wardrobe, then dropped to L, then M. The top comment: "Most expensive part of carnivore isn't the meat." So tell me, what's the most unexpected change you didn't plan for when you started?

key_insights:
# Marcus's Weekly Carnivore Content Analysis

## What the Numbers Say

Two videos broke 20k this week. Dr. Tony Hampton's electrolyte breakdown pulled 22,053 views with 235 comments, and the Keto Twins dessert video hit 20,576 views with a massive 2,447 likes. That's an 11.9% like ratio on the dessert content. People don't just watch recipe videos. They save them.

The Keto Twins also dropped an eating-out guide at 16,218 views and 1,814 likes. Two videos in the top 4 from one channel tells you they've figured out their formula: practical content that solves real problems.

Kent Carnivore's protein debate (10,761 views, 246 comments) had the highest raw comment count among mid-tier creators. Protein optimization is still a topic people will argue about for free.

But the real outlier? Ground Beef Chief's love story. Just 1,884 views but 174 comments. That's a 9.2% comment-to-view ratio. For context, anything above 2% is considered strong engagement. This guy is running at 4x that benchmark.

## This Week's Signal

Three patterns are impossible to ignore right now:

1. **Practical content wins the algorithm.** The top 3 videos by views are all how-to formats (electrolytes, desserts, eating out). Not debates. Not vlogs. Tactical stuff.

2. **Transformation stories win the community.** Reddit's top carnivore post this week was a 95-lb weight loss with medication freedom (388 upvotes). Ground Beef Chief's personal milestone got 174 comments on under 2k views. The OMAD plates post (292 upvotes) and the "clothes don't fit" humble brag (236 upvotes) confirm it. People want proof this works.

3. **Electrolytes aren't going away.** Dr. Hampton pulling 22k on an electrolyte video in 2026 tells you this is still a top-3 pain point for carnivore beginners. Every new person who starts this diet hits the same wall.

## The Opportunity

The gap between what performs on YouTube (practical how-tos, 20k+ views) and what performs on Reddit (transformation proof, 300+ upvotes) is where the content opportunity sits. Creators who combine both, showing the protocol AND the results, will own this space. Chris Cooking Nashville's meal system video (5,770 views, 542 likes) is the closest thing to that hybrid format this week. The audience is telling us exactly what they want: show me what to do, then prove it works.

qa_section.question: A man on Reddit dropped his A1C from 7.4 to 4.1 and quit six medications after losing 95 lbs on carnivore. Is that kind of metabolic turnaround realistic?
qa_section.answer: It's real, and it's more common than most people think. An A1C of 7.4 means average blood sugar was around 166 mg/dL. At 4.1, that's down to roughly 68 mg/dL, which is solidly non-diabetic. What's happening is straightforward: when you remove the carbohydrate load, your pancreas doesn't need to pump out as much insulin, and your cells start responding to insulin again. A 2021 study in the Journal of Metabolic Health found that very low carbohydrate diets produced A1C reductions of 1-2 points within 6 months in type 2 diabetics. A 3.3-point drop is on the high end, but 95 lbs of fat loss amplifies everything. Less visceral fat means less inflammatory signaling, better hepatic insulin sensitivity, and lower fasting glucose. The medication reductions make sense too, because the conditions the pills were treating (high blood sugar, high blood pressure, inflammation) often improve or resolve when the metabolic root cause gets addressed. That said, if you're on medications, don't stop them on your own. Work with your doctor and let your bloodwork guide the tapering.

citations.authors: Athinarayanan SJ, Adams RN, Hallberg SJ, et al.
citations.summary: Two-year trial showing sustained A1C reductions and medication elimination in type 2 diabetics following a very low carbohydrate diet with medical supervision.

citations.title: Dietary carbohydrate restriction as the first approach in diabetes management
citations.authors: Feinman RD, Pogozelski WK, Astrup A, et al.
citations.summary: Consensus statement from 26 researchers establishing carbohydrate restriction as the most evidence-supported intervention for type 2 diabetes management.

qa_section.caveats: If you take diabetes medications, especially insulin or sulfonylureas, reducing carbs without medical supervision can cause dangerous hypoglycemia. Always work with your doctor to adjust medications as your bloodwork improves.

qa_section.question: People in the Reddit comments keep arguing about fat-to-protein ratios. How much protein do you actually need on carnivore, and can you eat too much?
qa_section.answer: The short answer: most people aren't eating enough protein, not too much. A good starting point is 1.0 to 1.2 grams per pound of lean body mass. So if you weigh 200 lbs at 30% body fat, that's about 140-168 grams of protein per day. The "too much protein raises blood sugar" worry comes from a misunderstanding of gluconeogenesis. Your body can convert protein to glucose, but it's a demand-driven process, not a supply-driven one. Eating an extra steak doesn't spike your blood sugar the way eating a bowl of rice does. A 2013 study confirmed that high-protein meals don't produce significant glucose or insulin spikes in people without diabetes. The fat-to-protein ratio debate gets loud because people feel different at different ratios. Someone who's metabolically healthy and active will likely do well eating leaner. Someone who's still insulin resistant might feel better with more fat and slightly less protein because fat blunts the insulin response. There's no universal ratio. Pay attention to your satiety, your energy, and your bloodwork.

citations.title: An increase in dietary protein improves the blood glucose response in persons with type 2 diabetes
citations.authors: Gannon MC, Nuttall FQ, Saeed A, et al.
citations.summary: Found that protein ingestion stimulates insulin secretion but does not produce a significant increase in blood glucose concentration.

citations.title: Gluconeogenesis and energy expenditure after a high-protein, carbohydrate-free diet
citations.authors: Veldhorst MA, Westerterp-Plantenga MS, Westerterp KR
citations.summary: Demonstrated that gluconeogenesis increases on high-protein diets but is demand-driven, not causing blood glucose elevations in healthy subjects.

qa_section.caveats: People with kidney disease should consult their nephrologist before starting a high-protein diet. For everyone else, healthy kidneys handle protein intake well, but get your baseline kidney markers checked so you have a reference point.

qa_section.question: I'm doing OMAD on carnivore and losing weight fast. Is there a point where weight loss is too rapid, and should I be worried about anything?
qa_section.answer: Rapid weight loss in the first few weeks is mostly water. When you cut carbs, your body dumps glycogen stores, and each gram of glycogen holds about 3 grams of water. It's not unusual to lose 10-15 lbs in the first two weeks, and that's not fat loss, it's fluid rebalancing. After that initial phase, losing 2-3 lbs per week is common on OMAD carnivore, especially if you have a lot to lose. That rate is generally fine. Where it gets concerning is if you're losing muscle along with fat. OMAD can work well, but you need to hit your protein target in that single meal. If your plate is 80% fat and you're only getting 60 grams of protein, you'll lose weight on the scale but some of it will be lean tissue. A 2020 review found that time-restricted eating preserves lean mass as long as protein intake stays adequate, roughly 1.0g per pound of target body weight. The other thing to watch is electrolytes. Rapid water loss means rapid mineral loss. If you're getting cramps, headaches, or heart palpitations, your sodium and potassium are probably low. The Reddit joke about clothes not fitting is real. Budget for a belt hole punch.

citations.title: Effects of time-restricted eating on body weight and metabolism
citations.summary: Review showing time-restricted eating can produce significant fat loss while preserving lean mass when protein intake is sufficient.

citations.title: Glycogen storage capacity and de novo lipogenesis during massive carbohydrate overfeeding in man
citations.authors: Acheson KJ, Schutz Y, Bessard T, et al.
citations.summary: Established the relationship between glycogen storage and water retention, explaining the rapid initial weight loss seen when carbohydrates are restricted.

qa_section.caveats: If you feel dizzy, have persistent heart palpitations, or your hair starts thinning significantly, slow down and talk to your doctor. Rapid weight loss can also release stored toxins from fat tissue and affect gallbladder function, so don't ignore symptoms that feel off.
